title: Chat application
scopeHtml: Scope: 1:1 and group rooms, observer delivery, mediator service, per-room ordering. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design the LLD of a chat application: register users, send 1:1 and group messages, deliver them to members, and fetch recent history. Network transport (WebSockets) is out of scope; we model the objects and the delivery logic.

Clarify:

  • Functional: 1:1 chat, group chat, message history (last N), only members may post.
  • Not now: media, read receipts, end-to-end encryption, presence.
  • Scale talk: WhatsApp reported around 100 billion messages a day; a single group is at most a few hundred (WhatsApp cap was 1,024 members at the time of writing, confirm current). Per-conversation logic is small; the system is hard because of fan-out and connections.

Worked example. A group of 200 members and 1 message per second per active group: 199 deliveries per second for that one group. 10,000 such groups is about 2M deliveries per second, which is why real systems shard by conversation.

Industry examples. WhatsApp runs Erlang servers holding millions of connections each; Slack and Discord model everything as a channel, and a DM is a channel of two. Kafka or similar logs store ordered messages per conversation.

Everyday analogy. A notice board per room: anything pinned is copied into each member's pigeonhole.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing separate code paths for 1:1 and group.
  • Skipping the membership check.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• User (name, inbox, implements listener).
  • ChatRoom (id, members, history). A 1:1 chat is a room of two.
  • Message (id, from, text, timestamp); immutable record.
  • ChatService: registers users, creates rooms, sends, reads history.

Decision gravity. "1:1 is a 2-member room" removes a whole class of duplicate code. Reversible: yes. The room id for a pair is the sorted pair of names so direct(a, b) and direct(b, a) return the same room.

Everyday analogy. A DM is just a very small group.

Common interview traps.

  • Two different message tables or classes for DM and group.
  • Message ids from System.currentTimeMillis(); they collide. Use a sequence.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+-------------+  *   * +-----------+ 1    * +-----------+
| User        |<-------| ChatRoom  |------->| Message   |
| name        | members| id        |history | id from   |
| inbox       |        +-----------+        | text ts   |
+-------------+                             +-----------+
      ^ implements
<<ChatListener>> onMessage(room, msg)

ChatService: register, createGroup, direct, send, lastN

Common interview traps.

  • Making Message mutable so a later edit rewrites history.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Observer: users implement ChatListener; the room pushes each message to every member. In production the listener is a WebSocket connection or a push-notification (FCM/APNs) sender.
  • Mediator: ChatService and ChatRoom sit between users so users never hold references to each other. Alternative: users call each other, which creates a mesh of N squared links.
  • Immutable value object for Message.
  • Reversible: yes. The one-way door is the message id and ordering scheme once data is stored.

Worked example. asha posts to "team" (asha, ben, cy): ben and cy get it, asha does not get her own echo. Output shows cy's inbox [team] asha: standup now.

Industry examples. Slack fans out via a pub/sub per channel; Discord uses per-guild state and Elixir/Erlang style processes; WhatsApp stores messages on the server only until delivery.

Everyday analogy. A post office (mediator): you hand letters to it, never to each recipient.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending to the sender too.
  • Letting users be notified before the message is stored (a crash then loses it).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;

record Message(long id, String from, String text, long ts) {}

interface ChatListener { void onMessage(String room, Message m); }

class User implements ChatListener {
    final String name; final List<String> inbox = new ArrayList<>();
    User(String n) { name = n; }
    public void onMessage(String room, Message m) { inbox.add("[" + room + "] " + m.from() + ": " + m.text()); }
}

class ChatRoom {
    final String id; final Map<String, User> members = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    final List<Message> history = new ArrayList<>();
    ChatRoom(String id) { this.id = id; }
}

class ChatService {
    private final Map<String, User> users = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, ChatRoom> rooms = new HashMap<>();
    private long seq = 0;

    User register(String name) { return users.computeIfAbsent(name, User::new); }

    ChatRoom createGroup(String id, String... names) {
        ChatRoom r = new ChatRoom(id);
        for (String n : names) r.members.put(n, users.get(n));
        rooms.put(id, r); return r;
    }
    ChatRoom direct(String a, String b) {          // 1:1 is just a 2-member room
        String id = a.compareTo(b) < 0 ? a + "|" + b : b + "|" + a;
        ChatRoom r = rooms.get(id);
        return r != null ? r : createGroup(id, a, b);
    }
    void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
        ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
        if (!r.members.containsKey(from)) throw new SecurityException("not a member");
        Message m = new Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
        r.history.add(m);
        for (User u : r.members.values()) if (!u.name.equals(from)) u.onMessage(roomId, m);
    }
    List<Message> lastN(String roomId, int n) {
        List<Message> h = rooms.get(roomId).history;
        return h.subList(Math.max(0, h.size() - n), h.size());
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ChatService s = new ChatService();
        User a = s.register("asha"), b = s.register("ben"), c = s.register("cy");
        s.register("zed");
        s.createGroup("team", "asha", "ben", "cy");
        s.send("team", "asha", "standup now");
        ChatRoom d = s.direct("ben", "asha");
        s.send(d.id, "ben", "ok coming");
        System.out.println(a.inbox); System.out.println(c.inbox);
        try { s.send("team", "zed", "hi"); throw new AssertionError(); }
        catch (SecurityException e) { System.out.println("blocked non-member"); }
        System.out.println(s.lastN("team", 5).size());
    }
}

Kotlin core:

data class Message(val id: Long, val from: String, val text: String, val ts: Long)

class User(val name: String) {
    val inbox = mutableListOf<String>()
    fun onMessage(room: String, m: Message) { inbox += "[$room] ${m.from}: ${m.text}" }
}

class ChatRoom(val id: String, val members: Map<String, User>) {
    val history = mutableListOf<Message>()
}

class ChatService {
    private val users = mutableMapOf<String, User>()
    private val rooms = mutableMapOf<String, ChatRoom>()
    private var seq = 0L
    fun register(n: String) = users.getOrPut(n) { User(n) }
    fun createGroup(id: String, vararg names: String) =
        ChatRoom(id, names.associateWith { users.getValue(it) }).also { rooms[id] = it }
    fun send(roomId: String, from: String, text: String) {
        val r = rooms.getValue(roomId)
        require(from in r.members) { "not a member" }
        val m = Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis())
        r.history += m                                    // store first, then deliver
        r.members.values.filter { it.name != from }.forEach { it.onMessage(roomId, m) }
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing storage and delivery so a slow user blocks others.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
[[asha|ben] ben: ok coming]
[[team] asha: standup now]
blocked non-member
1

Test: non-member rejected, no echo to sender, direct(a,b) equals direct(b,a), lastN with N larger than history.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing that order is preserved.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Problems in the simple version: seq increments race (duplicate ids), history (ArrayList) is corrupted by concurrent adds, and a slow listener blocks the sender.

Thread-safe version.

class ChatRoom {
    final Map<String, User> members = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<Message> history = new ArrayList<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // per room: order within a room

    Message append(String from, String text, AtomicLong ids) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Message m = new Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
            history.add(m);                    // order of history == order of ids inside this room
            return m;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

// delivery is OUTSIDE the lock, on an executor
void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
    Message m = r.append(from, text, ids);
    for (User u : r.members.values())
        if (!u.name.equals(from)) pool.execute(() -> u.onMessage(roomId, m));
}

The per-room lock guarantees one total order per conversation, which is the guarantee users actually notice. Global ordering across rooms is not needed. User inbox should be a ConcurrentLinkedQueue.

Production note (gravity). Distributed: one conversation maps to one shard/partition (Kafka key = room id) so a single consumer orders it. Choosing the partition key is a one-way door. Delivery is at-least-once, so clients dedupe by message id.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global lock for the whole service.
  • Delivering while holding the room lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Offline users: store undelivered messages, deliver on reconnect (queue per user).
  • Read receipts and typing: more event types on the same Observer.
  • Pagination: history(before=id, limit=50).
  • Mute, block, admin roles: permission check in send.
  • Search: inverted index per room.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising exactly-once delivery; say at-least-once plus dedupe.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• 1:1 chat is a 2-member room; one code path.
  • Observer for delivery, mediator service in the middle, immutable messages.
  • Store first, then deliver; never echo to sender.
  • Thread safety: per-room lock for ordering, atomic ids, deliver outside the lock.
  • At scale: shard by conversation, at-least-once with client dedupe.
